catalog_quote: Stress is always on the first syllable of the word and is indicated by higher pitch and loudness. Since it is regular I do not write it in the phonetic transcription. The intonation drops from the first syllable towards the end of the word, except in polar questions where the intonation is falling-rising on the last syllable of the final word of the clause. Pinai-Hagahai is not a tonal language.

new_statements.relation_note: Language is not in the catalog and has no existing statements; this is the first placement statement found (fixed initial stress, non-tonal). Compatible with the stress-marked wordlists already held by the project (Davies & Comrie 1985 appendix) which carry marks but no rule. Description is explicitly of the Pinai dialect (p. 305); the Luya-Ginam(-Mamusi) dialect is only compared lexically/segmentally in 3.3, with no separate stress statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed and predictable on the first syllable of the word, realised as higher pitch and loudness; because it is fully regular the author omits it from transcriptions (and uses stress as a criterion for phonological word breaks, marked #, p. 305-306). The language is explicitly not tonal; word-level pitch falls from the first syllable, with a falling-rising contour on the clause-final syllable only in polar questions.
new_statements.exceptions: None; stress is stated to be 'always' initial and 'regular'. Only intonational exception: falling-rising contour on the last syllable of the clause-final word in polar questions (intonation, not stress).
new_statements.identity_note: Melliger 2005 explicitly describes the Pinai dialect of Pinai-Hagahai (p. 305: 'This paper is a description of the phonology essentials of the Pinai dialect'); the other dialect, Luya-Ginam(-Mamusi) ('Hagahai' side, Madang Province), is treated only in a brief lexical/segmental comparison (sec. 3.3) with no separate stress statement. Data: c. 1000 unelicited sentences from 90 recorded texts plus c. 2000 elicited items, author's own SIL fieldwork; ms. dated December 2003, published 2005.

tone.says: Tone reported absent: sec. 4 'Suprasegmentals' (p. 306) states that stress is always on the first syllable of the word, realised as higher pitch and loudness and therefore left unwritten; intonation falls from the first syllable to the end of the word except for a falling-rising contour on the last syllable of the clause-final word in polar questions (exx. 2-5, pp. 306-307); 'Pinai-Hagahai is not a tonal language.' No lexical or grammatical tone contrasts anywhere in the 36-page description.

sources.citation: Davies, John & Bernard Comrie. 1985. A linguistic survey of the Upper Yuat. In K. Adams et al. (eds), Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 22, 275-312. Pacific Linguistics A-63. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: No statement about stress anywhere in the article (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text for stress/accent/prosody: nothing). The Appendix wordlists (pp. 283-312) transcribe Pinai 1, Pinai 2, Nangenuwetan, Aramo and Wiyaw forms with a stress tick before the stressed syllable (e.g. Pinai 1 'head'..bo'E, 'mouth' ma bu'ra; Aramo place names ['ruja], [ma'ragia] on p. 279) but no conventions note or rule is given. Establishes Pinai and Nangenuwetan as dialects of one language, Aramo a distinct language (Pia subfamily of Piawi), and Pinai != Wapi (Enga).
